questions.q: What is the defining feature of WebSockets compared with HTTP request/response?
options: Guaranteed reliable message delivery with broker-grade acknowledgement semantics
Automatic reconnection managed entirely by the browser runtime
Text-only frames, making binary data transfer impossible
A persistent bidirectional connection where either side sends anytime
questions.explanation: WebSockets replace the strict request-response cycle with a full-duplex framed channel, so the server can push without being asked. Reconnection and delivery guarantees are left to the application.

questions.q: What is Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
options: A UDP-based push channel offering at-most-once delivery
A long-lived HTTP response streaming server-to-client events
A bidirectional binary protocol negotiated via HTTP upgrade
A polling convenience library that ships built into every modern browser
questions.explanation: SSE is ordinary HTTP: the server responds with text/event-stream and never closes the body, appending newline-delimited events as they occur.

questions.q: What is short polling's main inefficiency?
options: Many requests return empty because nothing changed between polls
Each poll permanently invalidates the server's response cache
Polling requires sticky sessions to be configured on every load balancer
Responses cannot be compressed when requests are repeated
questions.explanation: Polling decouples request rate from event rate, so when updates are rare most requests pay full connection, header, and auth cost to learn that nothing happened.

questions.q: How does long polling differ from short polling?
options: It opens one connection per event type instead of one connection total
It polls on a fixed schedule but batches multiple responses together
The server holds the request open until data arrives or a timeout hits
It uses HTTP/2 push frames instead of ordinary responses
questions.explanation: Long polling trades an idle held request for near-instant delivery: the response is deferred until there is something to say, then the client immediately reissues.

questions.q: Which transport is one-directional (server to client) by design?
options: WebSocket connections
SSE event streams
WebRTC data channels
Raw TCP socket links
questions.explanation: SSE is a streaming HTTP response, so data only flows downstream; anything the client wants to send goes over a separate ordinary HTTP request.

questions.q: Which use case most clearly needs WebSockets rather than SSE?
options: A news ticker pushing fresh headlines to readers
A monitoring dashboard streaming server CPU metrics down to viewers
A stock price feed updating a user's watch list
A multiplayer game sending frequent input in both directions
questions.explanation: Only the game needs low-latency client-to-server traffic. The other three are pure server-push feeds that SSE handles with less machinery.

questions.q: Built-in reconnection with Last-Event-ID resume is a native feature of which transport?
options: WebSockets, via the browser's socket API
Short polling, via ETag revalidation
SSE, via the browser's EventSource API
gRPC streams, via HTTP/1.1 trailers
questions.explanation: EventSource reconnects automatically and replays the last event id it saw in a Last-Event-ID header, letting the server resume the stream. WebSocket clients must implement this themselves.

questions.q: Why do WebSockets complicate classic HTTP load balancing?
options: Connections are long-lived and stateful, so per-request balancing no longer applies
Load balancers cannot parse WebSocket URLs because those URLs omit the scheme entirely
Each frame requires a fresh TLS handshake at the balancer
WebSockets bypass DNS and connect by raw IP address only
questions.explanation: A balancer normally rebalances every request, but a socket is pinned to one backend for hours, so load skews and deploys, drains, and scaling all become harder.

questions.q: 10k dashboard viewers need server metrics every 2 seconds, with no client-to-server messages. Best fit?
options: SSE: simple HTTP, native reconnection, one direction matches the need
WebSockets: bidirectionality is required for acknowledgements
Short polling every 2 seconds, since it holds far fewer connections than streaming
WebRTC: peer-to-peer delivery offloads the server entirely
questions.explanation: The traffic is pure server push, so SSE's one-way model fits exactly while keeping normal HTTP infrastructure, auth, and free automatic reconnection.

questions.q: Long polling runs behind a proxy with a 30-second idle timeout. What is the symptom and fix?
options: Every request is rejected instantly; enabling HTTP/2 bypasses the proxy's idle timeouts
The proxy caches the empty responses; disable caching for that URL
Held requests die at 30s; set the poll timeout below the proxy's and reissue
Clients receive duplicate responses; deduplicate using response ETags
questions.explanation: A held request looks idle to the proxy and is killed mid-flight. Returning an empty 200 just under the proxy limit turns a hard error into a clean re-poll.

questions.q: A server holds one million concurrent WebSocket clients. What is the dominant cost?
options: CPU consumed by continuously re-parsing full HTTP headers on every single frame
Disk I/O from journaling every frame for later replay
TLS re-handshakes, which recur every few seconds per client
Memory and file descriptors for every open connection's state
questions.explanation: Mostly idle sockets consume almost no CPU, but each still holds an fd plus kernel and TLS buffers, so per-connection memory and fd limits set the ceiling.

questions.q: You are deploying new code to servers holding WebSocket connections. What must the rollout handle?
options: Nothing special, because load balancers transparently replay in-flight frames after restarts
Draining: notify clients and let them reconnect elsewhere before instance shutdown
Doubling connection limits so the old and new versions can share sockets
Pausing DNS resolution so no new clients arrive during the deploy
questions.explanation: Long-lived sockets cannot survive a process restart, so graceful shutdown means stopping new accepts and closing existing ones gradually to avoid a reconnect storm.

questions.q: In a chat app, messages must reach users connected to other server instances. Standard architecture?
options: Instances write messages to shared disk, which peers poll for changes
Each client opens one socket per online friend for direct delivery
A gossip protocol running between browsers propagates the messages
A pub/sub backplane (e.g., Redis) fans messages out across instances
questions.explanation: Since a recipient's socket may live on any instance, each server subscribes to the relevant channels and the broker fans out, decoupling senders from connection placement.

questions.q: Why can SSE over HTTP/1.1 hit browser connection limits, and what helps?
options: Browsers cap ~6 connections per host; HTTP/2 multiplexing lifts the constraint
SSE reserves two dedicated sockets per stream; disabling automatic retries frees one of them
EventSource forbids concurrent streams; web workers can add more
Proxies collapse SSE streams per origin; unique query strings help
questions.explanation: Each SSE stream permanently occupies one of the ~6 per-origin HTTP/1.1 sockets, starving normal requests. Over HTTP/2 all streams share one multiplexed connection.

questions.q: Mobile clients use WebSockets on flaky networks. Which client-side mechanisms are essential?
options: Immediate zero-delay reconnect loops, minimizing the number of missed frames
Heartbeats to detect dead links, jittered backoff reconnects, and resume from the last message
Switching to raw TCP, which the operating system reconnects automatically
Longer TLS session tickets so that reconnects can skip DNS resolution
questions.explanation: Silently dead TCP connections need heartbeats to detect, jittered backoff prevents synchronized reconnect storms, and cursor-based resume closes the gap in missed messages.

questions.q: When does short polling actually beat a streaming transport?
options: When updates are frequent and every millisecond of latency matters
When the server cannot set custom HTTP headers on its responses
Infrequent updates with cheap cacheable responses and simple infrastructure
When the clients are mostly desktop browsers rather than mobile
questions.explanation: When staleness of a minute is acceptable, polling is stateless, cache-friendly, and trivially load balanced, avoiding all the connection-state cost of streaming.

questions.q: 500k connections, heartbeats every 30s, pushes are rare. What dominates capacity and how do you scale?
options: Bandwidth dominates; add compression to shrink the heartbeat frames
CPU dominates; move heartbeat handling onto GPU worker threads
Idle connection state dominates; scale on memory and FD limits, tune keepalive intervals
Disk dominates; heartbeats are journaled and need faster SSDs
questions.explanation: With rare pushes and tiny heartbeats, throughput is negligible; the binding constraint is per-socket memory and descriptors, so capacity planning targets those.

questions.q: A gateway restart triggers 300k simultaneous reconnects. Which mitigations address the thundering herd?
options: Jittered client backoff, staggered drains, and connection-rate limits at the edge
Reject every reconnect attempt for ten full minutes so the herd disperses naturally
Switch all clients to short polling permanently after any disconnect
Increase heartbeat frequency so dead clients are detected faster
questions.explanation: The fix is spreading the load in time: randomized backoff desynchronizes clients, staggered draining avoids dropping everyone at once, and rate limits protect handshake capacity.

questions.q: A client disconnects for 20 seconds during a live auction. What design avoids missed bids?
options: Nothing is needed, since TCP itself guarantees delivery of every bid
Server-side buffering keyed by stream position so clients resume with replay
Reducing the heartbeat interval to one second so disconnects cannot happen
Sending each bid twice over two separate sockets for redundancy
questions.explanation: TCP guarantees nothing once the connection dies. Keeping a per-stream sequence number lets a reconnecting client say where it left off and receive the gap.

questions.q: Why does SSE often work through strict enterprise middleboxes where WebSockets fail?
options: SSE frames are encrypted at a layer that proxies cannot inspect
WebSockets always use nonstandard ports that corporate firewalls block by default
SSE traffic is whitelisted automatically under IANA registry rules
SSE is plain HTTP, while the WebSocket Upgrade handshake gets dropped by strict intermediaries
questions.explanation: SSE is just a long HTTP response any proxy understands, whereas the Upgrade handshake switches to a non-HTTP framing that older or strict intermediaries refuse to pass.
